# Osmo's Coded Canvas: A New Blueprint for Corporate Storytelling?  
**SAN FRANCISCO, CA – August 05, 2026** – In the relentless arms race for audience attention, corporate storytellers have been handed a powerful but deeply flawed weapon: generative artificial intelligence. The promise was a firehose of video content, but the reality has been a deluge of what one industry insider terms "more slop, faster"—generic, off-brand, and often uneditable media. Now, a new company, emerging from stealth with $5 million in seed funding, is proposing a fundamental architectural shift. Osmo, founded by a team with creative DNA from A24 and Saturday Night Live, is not just launching another AI tool; it's arguing for a new relationship between the creator and the machine.  
Today, the company announced the general availability of its video production platform, which it claims can fuse the accessibility of a simple design tool with the power of professional animation software. Backed by a funding round led by Bain Capital Ventures, Osmo is making a high-stakes bet that the future of enterprise video isn't about replacing human taste with an algorithm, but about giving it a more expressive and efficient canvas.
## The Structural Challenge Ahead  
Despite the compelling vision and strong initial backing, Osmo is entering a fiercely competitive arena. The path from a promising seed-stage company to an indispensable enterprise tool is fraught with structural challenges. The core innovation—generating editable code—must prove it can scale to handle the immense complexity of high-end animation without compromising the real-time performance that forms a key part of its value proposition. The system must be robust enough for power users while remaining accessible to the generalists it aims to empower.  
Furthermore, the creative technology landscape is not static. Incumbents like Adobe are aggressively integrating their own AI features, while a host of well-funded competitors, from RunwayML to Synthesys, are racing to capture the same market. Osmo’s differentiation is clear for now, but it will need to innovate continuously to maintain its edge. On a more practical level, the company faces the mundane but significant challenge of building a brand in a crowded space, a task complicated by sharing a name with a popular children's game and a line of camera equipment.

Every company has a storyteller. The person who can already picture a distinctive launch video, a vivid product reveal, or a powerful title sequence, fully formed in their head. For years, they've had...  
*Taste is for humans. The answer to AI slop isn't a smarter model. It's giving people a tool to express themselves freely*  
SAN FRANCISCO: Every company has a storyteller. The person who can already picture a distinctive launch video, a vivid product reveal, or a powerful title sequence, fully formed in their head. For years, they've had no way to make it real themselves. Video and motion design lived inside professional tools that take years to master, or behind a queue of specialists, or lately, inside a prompt box that promises to bottle taste inside an AI model.  
Today, [Osmo](https://cts.businesswire.com/ct/CT?id=smartlink&url=https%3A%2F%2Fosmo.inc%2F&esheet=54583732&newsitemid=20260805820358&lan=en-US&anchor=Osmo&index=1&md5=54102b10d9d7c977c0da80700419709f), the storytelling studio with a software factory, is making its end-to-end video product generally available to storytellers and GTM teams at high-growth companies. The company was founded by a team with backgrounds from A24, NBC, and Saturday Night Live. Osmo is also announcing a $5 million seed round led by Bain Capital Ventures, with participation from Basis Set Ventures, MVP Ventures, Collaborative Fund, Scott Belsky, and others.
Today’s generative AI video models are diffusion-based systems that give you a single fixed output. Current models spray out generic, off-brand media at volume. But “more slop, faster” is not what enterprise brands need.  
Osmo generates animations as editable code rather than fixed AI output. It combines the accessibility of Canva with the power of Adobe, giving storytellers complete authorship over the final result. So instead of handing users a finished video they can't change, Osmo enables them to build each piece in an editable, programmable way-more like a website than a traditional video. Users can bring together motion, visuals, footage, and other mixed media into a complete story, while keeping the text, colors, timing, movement, and brand rules editable through natural language from the start.  
The company created 50+ films in its first seven months, then turned what it learned into software that lets marketing and GTM leaders create complete videos for their storytelling needs. Leaders at Webflow, Resend, Rho, and Gumloop already rely on Osmo to produce videos with more creative control.  
With Osmo:  
“Taste shouldn't be owned by a committee of ‘tastemakers’ and locked inside a model. It should be expressed freely by every creator,” said Chris He, CEO and co-founder of Osmo. “Every person’s individual taste is irreducibly personal, and the moment you try to distill it into a dataset, you've already lost it.”
**About Osmo**  
Osmo is a film studio and software company that turns an idea into polished, production-quality videos. By generating animations as editable code rather than fixed AI output, Osmo pairs the accessibility of Canva with the power of Adobe and gives storytellers complete authorship over every frame. Founded by Chris He, Will Hoppin, Basil Alfaro and Oleksandr Shevenionov, Osmo builds the creative tools its own team always wished they had. Learn more at [https://osmo.inc](https://cts.businesswire.com/ct/CT?id=smartlink&url=https%3A%2F%2Fosmo.inc&esheet=54583732&newsitemid=20260805820358&lan=en-US&anchor=https%3A%2F%2Fosmo.inc&index=3&md5=89881917ec35f5a9a46739877b7207b6).
